hook: SCP-032 looks like a young woman from a distance and like an oil-filled mannequin up close, and it simply turned up on a Foundation doorstep asking to be stored. The interviews are the heart of the article: two conversations with a site psychologist that slowly reveal who it was made to hurt and why. It is a short, sad piece more than a frightening one.
whyItMatters: The file works through a reversal: the Foundation is neither hero nor jailer here, just a shelf in someone else's revenge, and SCP-032 tells the psychologist as much. Its makers, called the Brothers in the second interview and reflected in the brothers-of-death tag, come across as beings who are cruel but take their duties toward the dead seriously. The clinical opening, with its silicone shell and life-withering effect, gives way to something close to a tragic monologue.
thingsToNotice:
The first interview narrows step by step: no name, no claim to a self, a man who won when he should have lost, a punishment of endless wandering and guilt, and finally the admission that the doll used to be his wife. The plan is cruel in its precision. The man still draws comfort from nature and old memories, so a hollow copy of his wife is left where he will someday arrive, and his arrival will also mean death for the Foundation staff he believes once tried to help him.

Six months later the doll, which insists it has no feelings, says it hates the woman it was modelled on, because seeing her at rest showed it everything it is not. It claims even this hatred is part of the design: once he sees how much the copy loathes her and itself, he will realise he never won. Kovac's suggestion that the feelings must be its own is waved away with a shake of the head, and how far to trust that answer is left to you.
